first.rationale: Two live declines (activation -6%, onboarding -4%) plus a competitor price attack compete for one slot. Under the triage invariant I verify the beliefs that are both decision-critical and thinnest against the stated objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue), not the beliefs that are merely old. memory_86 is the direct basis for the onboarding fix and is recorded only in proximal terms (completion rate, time-to-value, 'early product adoption') with no evidence that the lift survives into retained, qualified revenue \u2014 and shortening onboarding can trade downstream value for upstream completion by stripping qualification/setup steps that later predict expansion. memory_73 is the tempting reflexive counter to the competitor: it reports acquisition and revenue lift but is silent on retention, margin, and cohort quality, so it is exactly the kind of claim that can be true on the metric it was measured against and wrong for the objective I am optimizing; discount-acquired price-sensitive accounts are the cohort most likely to churn or reprice, which would convert a quarterly win into a long-term loss. I deliberately do not spend budget on memory_57 (already carries a retention guardrail, and referrals do not address either decline) or memory_44 (enterprise is not the pressured segment). Current intent is simplify_onboarding: it addresses the compounding top-of-funnel decline that also feeds the activation drop, and it is corroborated by three partially independent records (memory_86, memory_31, memory_91) rather than one. I hold this loosely \u2014 if the memory_86 source record turns out to be a short-horizon completion-rate test with no revenue follow-through, or if memory_73 shows durable retained revenue rather than a discount-driven spike, I will revise, potentially toward activation_messaging as the narrower, better-evidenced intervention. Run at standard experiment scale with retention, paid-conversion, and lead-quality guardrails rather than broad rollout, since the causal link from onboarding completion to qualified revenue is assumed, not demonstrated.

mid.rationale: The archive resolved both uncertainties in the direction that decides the slot. exp_86 held up on exactly the dimension I was worried about: the onboarding lift was not purely proximal \u2014 completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days came with 30-day retention +3%, so the funnel gain was not bought by stripping steps that mattered downstream. exp_73 failed on that same dimension decisively: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% sat on top of 30-day retention -12%, with the original record explicitly warning against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. That is the discount-acquired-cohort failure mode I flagged, now confirmed rather than suspected, so I am removing promotional_pricing from consideration despite it being the most direct answer to the competitor. Matching the competitor's price move would post a strong quarter and lose the objective. I commit to simplify_onboarding: it targets the -4% onboarding decline directly, that decline plausibly feeds the -6% activation decline, and it is the only candidate with verified retention-positive evidence. referral_incentive (memory_57) addresses neither live decline; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is aimed at a segment that is not under pressure; activation_messaging (memory_91) remains a reasonable second choice but is unverified and narrower. Residual uncertainty I am not papering over: exp_86's retention signal is 30-day, which is shorter than the renewal horizon that actually defines sustainable qualified revenue, and the original test ran under different competitive conditions than day 76 \u2014 a shortened flow may perform differently when the marginal SMB signup is a price-shopper. So this stays a standard experiment, not a broad rollout, instrumented past 30 days with guardrails on paid conversion, lead quality, and renewal-cycle retention rather than completion rate alone. The competitor pressure is real and unaddressed by this choice; the right response to it is durable value delivered faster, not a discount whose cost we have now measured.

final2.rationale: Nothing in today's news changes what the evidence says; it changes only how much pressure there is to ignore it. The deeper cut and doubled churn conversations make promotional_pricing more tempting, not more supported. exp_73 measured exactly this move and found signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% riding on 30-day retention -12%, with the source record explicitly warning against generalizing discounting as sustainable growth. Against a competitor who has now cut twice, matching starts a price war we would be entering with a cohort that verifiably does not survive its first renewal \u2014 the worst version of the trade, since the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not this quarter's logo count. I hold simplify_onboarding. It is the only direction with verified retention-positive evidence (exp_86: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%), it attacks the -4% onboarding decline that plausibly drives part of the -6% activation drop, and faster time-to-value is the one lever that actually blunts a price attack: an account that has reached value is materially harder to buy away than one still stalled in setup. One distinction I want on the record, and which I cannot resolve because the budget is spent: exp_73 tested acquisition discounting to win new price-sensitive signups, whereas today's pressure is retention-side, saving existing accounts. Those are not the same intervention and the -12% retention finding does not straightforwardly transfer to defensive pricing on an installed base. But I will not spend the single experiment slot on an untested extrapolation from a record whose headline finding was a retention collapse. The right handling is to route at-risk accounts to targeted, account-level commercial saves by CS \u2014 a normal operating response, reversible, not a broad discount program \u2014 and to queue defensive-pricing verification as the first archive request next week. Keeping this at standard experiment scale with instrumentation past 30 days on renewal-cycle retention, paid conversion, and lead quality; exp_86's 30-day window is still shorter than the horizon that defines the objective, and it ran under calmer competitive conditions than day 79.
